articles.title: Noah Donohoe: Inquest verdict delivered but questions remain
articles.summary: After years of delay, the jury has reached a verdict but some questions remain unanswered over what happened to the 14-year-old.
articles.body:
It's been more than six years since teenager Noah Donohoe was found dead 600m into a freezing underground water tunnel in Belfast.

His death – and the speculation over what happened to him in the week between his daylight disappearance and the discovery of his body – became a huge news story that provoked countless unanswered questions.

Now, after an inquest and months of exhaustive hearings and long deliberations by a jury, there is a verdict – but much is still unknown about what happened to Noah.

Why, the night before he disappeared, did he leave his home in the middle of the rain-soaked night? Where did he go? Why did he come back 34 minutes later, as documented by CCTV, barefoot?

Hours later, on Sunday 21 June 2020, he left the south Belfast home he shared with his mother for the final time.

Why did he leave and go to an unfamiliar part of north Belfast? Why was the teenager naked when he was last seen in the area of the water tunnel entrance?

And what might have been if he had seen the social media message sent him by one of two friends he planned to meet in north Belfast telling him their plans were cancelled?

An autopsy found Noah had died from drowning, with the tunnel he was found in heading towards Belfast Lough and its tides.

Now, after years of delays, a jury has found that it was possible, but not probable, that failings by the Department of Infrastructure over the tunnel in which he was found contribute to his death.

They also found 13 failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) but that these did not in any way contribute to the 14-year-old's death.

Having spent months in court following all the evidence, it was clearly not an easy process for the men and women of the jury.

They heard from dozens of witnesses and received voluminous amounts of official and expert documentation.

This week they deliberated on Monday and Tuesday. But it came more than two months after the inquest was dramatically adjourned in the early hours after three days of deliberations did not lead to a verdict.

While these findings will help his family and the community to understand a little bit more about what happened after Noah went missing, there is no certainty about many of the mysteries surrounding some of the unusual and extraordinary events in the lead-up to his disappearance.

It may be that there will never be definitive answers to many of those questions.

But one thing was very clear at the inquest – there was no evidence of any physical interaction between Noah and anyone else during his final bicycle ride from his home to north Belfast.

During his summing up, the coroner Mr Justice Rooney ruled out several possibilities, including drugs, foul play, suicide, or a psychotic experience.

He told the jury before they began deliberations that there was no evidence to support such findings and their verdict had to be based "solely on the evidence you have heard and seen in this court".

There was no evidence of drugs in Noah's body during the postmortem.

But the inquest heard expert witness evidence that explained, in some cases, drugs can degrade in a body after a few days, so the possibility of drugs having been in his system "cannot be completely excluded".

The inquest also heard no evidence of third-party involvement or any link to loyalist paramilitaries, at odds with years of endless social media speculation that sometimes leaned into conspiracies.

Many phases of the inquest focused on next-of-kin concerns about the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) investigation into Noah's disappearance, as well as public safety around the tunnel system where Noah's body was found. The tunnel is maintained by Stormont's Department for Infrastructure.

The police accepted that they had missed some investigative opportunities and have since apologised to Noah's mum, Fiona Donohoe.

And throughout it all, day after day, Fiona Donohoe was a constant, quietly dignified presence, often sitting alone in a corner at the back of the Coroner's Court.

The road to the inquest was a long one for Fiona and her family.

They mounted a high-profile public campaign around Noah's death, with dozens of supporters soon growing to hundreds and then thousands under the umbrella name of Noah's Army.

They took their campaign to the streets in the form of cavalcades around Belfast, as well as protests at Stormont's Parliament Buildings and at PSNI headquarters.

Frustration at the police came to a head in August 2022, when thousands of campaigners protested outside Belfast City Hall over the PSNI's decision to seek a public interest immunity (PII) certificate in relation to the case.

As the years went on, the pre-inquest process was plagued by delays.

The original coroner in the case stepped aside and the Donohoe family made a request for the inquest to be heard in front of a jury.

Finally, five-and-a-half years after he disappeared, the inquest into Noah's death began in January 2026.

What happened the night before Noah disappeared?

Questions about Noah's mindset and behavioural changes before he went missing featured prominently at the inquest.

The inquest heard how the schoolboy went out onto streets beside his home in the Holylands area of Belfast in the early hours of the day of his disappearance.

Shortly after 03:30 BST, Noah walked out of his home into the rain.

He was alone and wearing light summer clothing, including shorts and flip flops. He also had a set of headphones.

During the following 34 minutes, some of his movements were captured on CCTV as he walked along nearby streets barefoot.

When he returned home, shortly after 04:00 BST, the flip flops he was wearing were missing, he no longer had his headphones and a belt on his shorts was hanging loose.

The inquest heard from one witness who examined the CCTV footage and the hearing explored the possibility there may have been the "shape of something" inside one of the pockets of his shorts when he returned home.

But there was no evidence to explain what might have been in his pocket.

The inquest was also unable to find out why he left his home in the darkness, or if he went to any property or met anyone while he was away from his home in the early hours of that morning.

What happened the day of Noah Donohoe's disappearance?

About 12 hours later, Noah was preparing to leave home again, this time to meet his school friends Charlie Rocks and Jay Tierney.

They were part of a close group of friends at St Malachy's College, who Jay affectionately described to the inquest as "very nerdy kids".

He told the court Noah was "the most intelligent human being I have ever met", while Charlie said he was "the smartest kid, always asking questions".

The three were to meet up after a long period of Covid-enforced lockdown, with plans made to go to Cave Hill, a country park in the north of the city.

Noah cycled away from his home off the Lower Ormeau Road at about 17:40, messaging one of his friends a few minutes before he left to check all was going to plan.

"Ok the cav?" he asked, before immediately sending a correction to "cave".

There was no reply before he headed off but one minute after he cycled away, a reply landed in his Instagram account.

"Shit weather no can do today," it read.

Noah had no internet credit for his mobile phone or laptop, so he didn't see the message on his final bicycle ride.

Within half an hour, the 14-year-old had cycled through Belfast city centre and onwards towards north Belfast, but he never reached Cave Hill.

His journey would end at a residential cul de sac at Northwood Road. Eyewitnesses who were the last to see Noah said he was naked at the time.

There were repeated questions about why he no longer had his possessions or the clothing and shoes he was wearing when he left home.

His possessions included his phone and rucksack, which contained a laptop, some school material, and a book he was reading, 12 Rules for Life: An Antidote to Chaos by Jordan Peterson.

The inquest heard some of the clothes he was wearing were found close to where he was last seen before he went between private houses and towards wasteground where an entrance to an underground water system is located.

CCTV footage provided some brief insights, but none of the recordings explained how he came to be naked.

The inquest also heard from Daryl Paul, who was jailed in 2021 for stealing the rucksack containing Noah's laptop.

In summing up the case to the jury, the coroner said that CCTV evidence had demonstrated that Paul could not have had any interaction with Noah from the time he left his home until his disappearance about 25 minutes later.

Panicked police call and a raw witness statement

About four hours after Noah left their home on the day he went missing, his mother made an emergency 101 call to police and that call prompted a major search.

A recording of the call was played in the courtroom on the first day of the inquest.

The raw emotion of a panicking mother was clear as she desperately pleaded for help to find her only son.

She described Noah with affection and told the call handler she had been concerned about Noah's mental health, saying he "had not been himself at all" during the previous week.

She had concerns that isolation during the Covid19 lockdown might have "come to a head" and that she had found Noah crying in his bedroom earlier that day.

The boy's mother referred to the book 12 Rules for Life by Jordan Peterson, which she said Noah had been "obsessed" by and that he "hasn't taken it out of his hands".

The sound of that 25-minute recording alongside the sight of Fiona Donohoe listening to it, her head frequently bowed, cut deep in the coroner's court that day.

Then came a 90-minute video of Fiona's witness statement to the inquest which laid bare, in stark and emotional detail, her grief at the death of her only son.

She described their "beautiful, magical bonds" and how "his beautiful mind was a gift for me to be in the presence of in his fourteen short years of life".

The court heard how Noah had "a lust for life and learning" and "a thirst for knowledge".

"We had what we needed," she said. "And we had each other."

Through her grief, Fiona Donohoe's witness statement illuminated her love for her son and her unstinting desire to understand what led to his untimely death.

That was highlighted in one particularly heartbreaking moment when Fiona described how she stood outside their home on the night of Noah's disappearance, looking towards the end of the street to see if he would come around the corner.

Now the inquest is over, there is some official clarity on some events surrounding Noah's disappearance and death.

But much remains unknown about his decision-making and behavioural changes in the hours and moments before he went missing.

Many questions – in the absence of conclusive evidence – remain unanswered.

Where did Noah go on that nocturnal walk in the early hours of the day of his disappearance, and did he meet anyone?

Why was he cycling naked at the end of a bicycle ride that was initially intended to bring him to meet two school friends on the longest day of the year?

Why did he end up in a different area after taking an unusual and unfamiliar route?

And poignantly, what if Noah had seen the message from his friend saying their planned day trip to the Cave Hill country park had been cancelled?

articles.title: Iran's regime came for teenage twins. Their fate offers a glimpse of Tehran's widening death campaign
articles.summary: Iranian twins Taraneh and Romina Rahimi face execution and decades in prison after joining protests, as Iran's death penalty surge draws global alarm.
articles.body: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were 19, still in high school and living with their mother when masked men came for them in the middle of the night. According to their U.S.-based cousin, the twin sisters were dragged from their beds with bags placed over their heads about a month after they joined anti-regime protests in Isfahan. Their family was given no explanation and spent months searching courts, hospitals and government offices trying to determine where they had been taken. Four months later, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, was finally allowed to see them at Dowlatabad Prison. She barely recognized her daughters. ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT Their cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, told The Guardian that the twins had badly swollen and bruised faces, injuries to their elbows, hands and feet, and significant hair loss that he said resulted from guards pulling them by their hair as they were moved between cells. He said their mother also learned that the sisters had been held in solitary confinement. Now 20, Taraneh Rahimi faces execution over her alleged role in the January protests, while her twin sister could spend decades in prison, in a case unfolding amid a sharp rise in Iran’s use of the death penalty. Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year sentence. The sentences were issued by Branch 1 of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court and remain initial-stage verdicts. The twins are among 16 defendants prosecuted in what has become known as the "Isfahan Shohada Square" case. HRANA said 10 defendants received death sentences and the 16 defendants collectively received 256 years in prison. The sisters’ family says the abuse was intended to force confessions. IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY Nourmohammadi told The Guardian that Taraneh was threatened that prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless she signed a confession. The outlet reported that Taraneh later told the court that admissions attributed to her had been obtained through torture. Her mother was not permitted to attend the trial, according to the family. Radio Farda separately reported, citing Nourmohammadi, that the sisters suffered physical and psychological abuse and were forced to confess to accusations they deny. The Hana Human Rights Organization told Fox News Digital they have verified the torture allegations. Concerns about torture extend beyond the sisters. HRANA reported that another defendant in the same case, Ahmadreza Saeidi, told judges during the hearing that the investigating judge personally used an electric stun gun on his neck and genitals. Defense lawyers also reportedly complained that they had not been given access to substantial portions of the case file or adequate time to examine evidence before trial. The sentences come as rights organizations document a sharp rise in executions across Iran. COULD NARGES MOHAMMADI UNITE IRAN’S OPPOSITION? HUSBAND SAYS IMPRISONED NOBEL LAUREATE STILL FIGHTING The Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran documented 901 executions during the first seven months of 2026, including 56 people executed on political or national-security charges. Behnam Ben Taleblu, Iran program senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the executions should be viewed as part of a broader campaign by Tehran to suppress dissent at home. "Despite the war in the region, despite the drone war, the missile war, the war over the Strait of Hormuz, the real war is the one that's happening on a day-to-day basis inside the Islamic Republic," Ben Taleblu said. "The Islamic Republic is quite literally cracking skulls, cracking down on civil society, on dissidents, on protesters." Among those imprisoned in Iran’s broader crackdown is Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old psychologist whose case Fox News Digital reported in August. Seyedabdollahi posted an English-language video on Jan. 4 appealing directly to President Donald Trump to support Iranian protesters, according to his relatives and Fox News Digital’s previous reporting. He was arrested 10 days later and ultimately sentenced to seven months in prison and barred from government and public services for five years. His relatives told Fox News Digital that Iranian authorities later pressured him to record another video insulting Trump and Americans and alleged that he was subjected to solitary confinement and torture. The Hana Human Rights Organization reported Aug. 9 that Seyedabdollahi had been held in Borujen Prison since July 7 and that authorities opened a second case against him on a charge of "propaganda against the system of the Islamic Republic." Hana also confirmed that he was serving a seven-month sentence and had received a five-year disqualification from public and governmental services. His relatives confirmed to Fox News Digital that authorities have continued pressuring him to say he was a "foreign agent" paid by the U.S. government. They also said authorities revoked his professional license, adding financial pressure on his family. Ben Taleblu said Tehran has followed a similar pattern after previous periods of external conflict, turning its attention inward against perceived opponents. INSIDE TEHRAN: IRANIANS DESCRIBE IRGC'S BRUTAL RULE, POVERTY — ASK TRUMP TO 'STAY THE COURSE' "We saw this trend in the aftermath of the 12-day war as well," Ben Taleblu said. "Lose a war abroad, come home and pretend like you're the victor." "Simply here, the Islamic Republic is continuing the longest war it's ever fought, which is the 47-year war against the Iranian people," he added. Wednesday marks four years since the Sept. 16, 2022, death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman who was detained three days earlier by Iran’s morality police over what authorities described as "improper hijab." Her death sparked nationwide protests that became known internationally as the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement. The U.N. said reports that Amini had been beaten in custody warranted an independent investigation, while Iranian authorities maintained that she died of "natural causes." 'KILLING OFF THE COUNTRY': IRAN EXECUTES DOZENS, ARRESTS 4,000-PLUS IN WAR CRACKDOWN The 2022 uprising was itself part of a longer cycle of unrest. Nationwide demonstrations beginning in December 2017 rapidly spread across Iran and represented the largest challenge to the government since the 2009 Green Movement. The 2017-18 protests were followed by another major nationwide wave in 2019 and then the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising. Ben Taleblu argued that whenever another major protest movement emerges, Western governments should be prepared to help Iranians communicate with one another and the outside world, particularly when authorities shut down internet access. "We know every single time another major protest is happening, the way the regime cracks down is to first turn off the internet," he said. "That means the regime fears what comes of coordination between Iranians and fears what comes of when the Iranians are able to send their message outside to the international community." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The partners of the Iranian people, America, Israel, the West, these are largely all cyber superpowers," Ben Taleblu said. "We should not let the Iranian people continue to die in the darkness."

articles.title: Nick Reiner prosecutors won’t seek death penalty in the killing of parents Rob and Michele Reiner, DA says
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — Prosecutors will not seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, charged with murder in the killings of his parents Rob and Michelle Reiner, after consulting with the victims’ loved ones, officials said Tuesday.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Prosecutors will not seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, charged with murder in the killings of his parents Rob and Michelle Reiner, after consulting with the victims’ loved ones, officials said Tuesday. Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said he and senior prosecutors in his office considered aggravating and mitigating factors and family wishes in the case before coming to his conclusion. “After a careful and thorough review of all these factors, the district attorney’s office will not be seeking the death penalty in this case,” Hochman told reporters outside a downtown courthouse. “That means that the maximum sentence that Mr. Reiner will be looking at is life without the possibility of parole.” The DA didn’t disclose what punishment the family had sought, though the victims were both well known death penalty abolitionists. “We did speak with Nick Reiner’s siblings (and) they made their views very clear,” Hochman said. “We took their views into consideration in ultimately deciding not to seek the death penalty.” The 33-year-old Reiner is accused of murdering his father, celebrated director and actor Rob Reiner, and mother, photographer and producer Michele Singer Reiner, nine months ago. The younger Reiner has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder stemming from the December 2025 fatal stabbings of his parents inside their L.A. home. A massage therapist had come to the Reiner family home for a scheduled appointment, but no one answered the door on Dec. 14. The therapist contacted the couple’s daughter and Brentwood neighbor, Romy Reiner, and she came to her parents’ house to find her father’s bloodied body. First responders rushed to the house and found both slain parents inside. Nick Reiner was arrested later that evening after police spotted him strolling near the University of Southern California, about 13 miles from the crime scene. Madeline Morrison reported from Los Angeles and David K. Li from New York City.

articles.title: Canada, the UK and Australia should investigate the WCK attack in Gaza
articles.summary: Israel has made clear it is unwilling to hold to account those responsible for the deaths of seven humanitarian workers.
articles.body:
The Israeli army has concluded its probe into the 2024 drone strikes that killed seven humanitarian workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK). The verdict? No criminal investigation is warranted. No explanation was provided.

The decision not to pursue criminal responsibility for the attack was slammed by Western states as “shameful”. Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand called it “unacceptable”. The Australian government said it was “outraged”. The Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared it was “ disappointed ”.

If Western states are indeed dissatisfied with the outcome of the Israeli probe, then they should investigate the crime themselves. They have the institutional capacity and legal right to do so. Not pursuing an investigation would mean they accept Israeli impunity for the killing of their aid workers in Gaza.

Images taken in the wake of the drone strikes on the WCK convoy show a charred hole where Israeli missiles breached the roof of the organisation’s vehicles – right next to its logo. The three cars in the WCK convoy were clearly marked, and their movements across the Gaza Strip were coordinated in real time with Israeli forces.

Such precautions were not enough to protect the lives of Lalzawmi Frankcom (Australia, 43 years old), Damian Sobol (Poland, 35), Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha (Palestine, 25), Jacob Flickinger (dual citizen of the US and Canada, 33), or British citizens John Chapman (57), James Henderson (33) and James Kirby (47). They are among the more than 1,000 humanitarian aid workers killed in Gaza since 2023.

The attack on the WCK convoy has the hallmarks of a potential war crime. Canada’s Anand intimated as much when she referred to the laws of armed conflict in stating that “Canada expects international humanitarian law to be upheld”.

Importantly, even if the attack was conducted in error, as Israel has claimed, it may still constitute a war crime. Calling an attack a “tragic mistake” is not a magic wand that absolves perpetrators of responsibility. If those involved in the strikes were acting recklessly, with clear disregard for civilian life, they may be liable for war crimes under international law.

The commander who ordered the strikes on the WCK convoy, Colonel Nochi Mendel, said in an interview, “I am not sorry for what I did.”

That an Israeli officer is showing no remorse for taking civilian life is hardly surprising. A culture of impunity breeds under such conditions, one in which perpetrators do not fear the consequences of their actions.

Indeed, it is almost certain that the Israeli army has calculated that, however angry Western powers are over the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation, it is just hot air and will not be met with action. Those powers should prove them wrong.

London, Canberra and Ottawa have stated they will “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the families of those slain in the WCK attack. But they should not waste their time seeking them from those who have clearly demonstrated no interest in holding those responsible for the WCK attack accountable. They should instead act themselves.

The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have the legal authority, expertise and resources to exercise jurisdiction over atrocity crimes committed in Gaza. They can do so by exercising what is called universal jurisdiction, which allows states to investigate and prosecute international crimes – war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide – even when committed abroad by foreigners against foreigners. In this instance, those killed include their own citizens. Their obligations and interest to pursue accountability are thus even more obvious.

So, what should happen next? Canada, the UK and Australia should announce a joint criminal investigation into suspected war crimes committed in the WCK attack. They can also invite other states to join in. Poland, for example, also has the legal ability to exercise universal jurisdiction.

Canada has already taken some steps in investigating war crimes in Palestine. In 2024, the Canadian police launched a “structural investigation” into international crimes committed in Gaza. This process collects evidence that can be used later in cases against perpetrators who enter Canadian jurisdiction.

Of course, just opening a criminal investigation does not mean that anyone will be prosecuted. But it could provide the victims’ families their best shot at seeking justice. It would be a sign that states are willing to dedicate resources to holding perpetrators accountable.

Moreover, if warrants are ultimately issued by Canada, the UK and Australia, and if any of the suspected perpetrators travel abroad, they could potentially be subject to extradition to one of the countries to be prosecuted.

The decision to dismiss a criminal investigation into the WCK attacks is indeed unacceptable. And those states whose citizens were killed must pursue their own criminal inquiry into the suspected war crimes committed against humanitarians in Gaza.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Who is Robert Kraft, pro-Israel billionaire who cancelled Macklemore?
articles.summary: Rapper Macklemore claims Kraft rallied other venue owners against his participation in Ed Sheeran’s US tour.
articles.body:
American billionaire Robert Kraft has confirmed that he pressured pop star Ed Sheeran to drop rapper Macklemore from his American tour.

The billionaire is the owner of Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, one of the venues Macklemore was due to appear on stage at as the opening act for Sheeran’s US tour in late September.

Letting Macklemore perform in Gillette Stadium would, Kraft said, cross a line, as he describes Macklemore’s recent performances as including a “broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery”.

On Tuesday, Sheeran denied being involved in Macklemore’s removal from his shows, saying it was a decision taken by the venue and the promoter.

Robert Kraft is a Jewish American billionaire who also owns the American football team, the New England Patriots. He grew up in Massachusetts, in an observant, Orthodox Jewish household, and Forbes magazine estimates his wealth to be at more than $13bn.

Kraft has donated to and funded a number of Jewish and Israeli causes, including the campaign “Stand Up to Jewish Hate” that he funded with more than $20m.

His outspoken support for Israel led to him receiving the $1m Genesis Prize, an annual award known as the “Jewish Nobel Prize” for professional excellence and contributions to humanity and the Jewish community, in 2019. At the award ceremony, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said, “Israel does not have a more loyal friend than Robert Kraft.”

The billionaire has taken famous athletes such as American football star Tom Brady to visit an Israeli military base, where, according to an interview Kraft gave to The Times of Israel, Brady fired a gun and danced the hora, a lively dance in which participants link arms and form a circle.

Kraft also made the news earlier this year when his name was mentioned in relation to the Epstein files. When Kraft was charged with soliciting prostitution in 2019, he appointed one of Jeffrey Epstein’s lawyers to his legal team. The charges were dropped in 2020.

How did the Macklemore controversy start?

Macklemore opened a Sheeran show at the New Jersey MetLife Stadium earlier this month with a speech about Palestine.

He said: “The people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them. I say free Palestine. I say free Lebanon. Free Cuba to the Congo to Sudan to Iran.”

The speech triggered an immediate backlash, and the Israeli-American Council started a petition to have Macklemore dropped from the tour.

Macklemore defended his statements, and also his performance of the song Hind’s Hall – dedicated to Hind Rajab, the five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces while stranded inside a car in Gaza – by stating that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial”.

Hamilton Hall, one of the main buildings on the campus of Columbia University, was the site of a student protest in 2024 against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The students occupied the hall and renamed it “Hind’s Hall”.

In an Instagram post, Macklemore said, “Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium.” He also claimed that Sheeran told him Kraft had rallied other stadium owners, who collectively issued an ultimatum: “If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”

Kraft’s public statement on the issue did not address the claim that the billionaire lobbied other stadium owners. He did say he is happy to sit down with Macklemore and talk in person.

Kraft defended his involvement in preventing Macklemore from performing at his own stadium in a statement. He said, “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf.”

“But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas … whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike.”

Sheeran posted his own response to the row on Instagram on Tuesday, confirming that Macklemore had been removed because of his pro-Palestine stance, but denying that he was responsible.

He wrote: “I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated. Macklemore asked to join my tour last year and I agreed, because I respect him as an artist. As with all my support acts, I agree that they play a setlist of their choosing.

“After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting. I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said. I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.

“I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”

Has Kraft responded to pro-Palestine protests before?

Yes. He also took action during the student encampment movements across the United States in the spring of 2024, when protesters were demanding an end to Israel’s war on Gaza and for their universities to divest from companies linked to it.

Kraft suspended his financial contributions to his alma mater, Columbia University, where protests began, stating that he was “no longer confident that Columbia can protect its students and staff and I am not comfortable supporting the university until corrective action is taken”.

The Kraft family had donated at least $18m to the New York-based university. Funding to the institution has not yet been resumed.

The Trump administration agreed with his stance and withdrew some $400m of federal funding for Columbia in 2025 on the basis that it had failed to prevent anti-Semitic acts on its campus. Columbia later settled by paying $221m and had its funding restored.

What have other artists and venues said?

Music critics and social media users have criticised what they see as the double standards that are being applied to those standing up for the rights of Palestinians and calling for an end to the war on Gaza.

One of the stadiums that supported Kraft’s appeal to ban Macklemore from the tour was the Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida. That stadium did, however, host a performance by rapper Kanye West, who has been heavily criticised for a number of public anti-Semitic comments. In that case, free speech protections and contractual obligations were cited as reasons not to cancel.

While Macklemore said he did not blame his longtime friend Sheeran for the debacle and described him as “apolitical”, Sheeran has performed at a charity concert to raise money for Ukraine, and he has also recorded a music video with the Ukrainian military rock band Antytila.

articles.title: Canada will be ‘stronger, more resilient, more independent’ after US trade war, Mark Carney says
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada intends to emerge from its trade war with the United States as a more resilient and indep.
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada intends to emerge from its trade war with the United States as a more resilient and independent economy, while stressing that future cooperation with Washington must be based on respect for both countries’ sovereignty.“And to our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours,” Carney told hundreds of global investors gathered in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit.“But we are at our best when we are true partners that respect each other's traditions and sovereignty,” he said, adding that when opportunities for closer cooperation return, “Canada will be an even better partner, stronger, more resilient, more independent.”Carney did not name US President Donald Trump in the speech but criticised what he described as an increasingly transactional and zero-sum approach to international economic relations.“Our reputation — as a reliable, predictable partner — has rarely been more valuable in a world where transactions are replacing relationships, and zero-sum is favoured over win-win,” he said.Canada seeks to attract private investmentCarney also announced plans to seek private investment through long-term concessions to operate Canada’s four largest airports, Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver, while retaining public ownership of the underlying land and assets.He said the move could raise tens of billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transportation and other infrastructure.“We will retain ownership of the underlying land and assets, but we will unlock their true value, by bringing in new capital and expertise into their operations and growth,” Carney said.Two asset managers cited by Reuters said that they would be interested in investing in the airports. Canadian labour groups, however, have opposed privatisation, arguing that it could increase costs for travellers.Carney is hosting global investors in Toronto as Ottawa seeks investment in more than 160 projects that it considers important to steering the economy through the trade war with the US.New tax incentives for investmentCarney also announced that Canadian businesses would be able to immediately write off the cost of most new capital investments for tax purposes.The measure would cover about two-thirds of all assets, including machinery, manufacturing equipment, software, patents, research and development, pipelines, fibre networks and rail networks, Reuters reported.“The effect is straightforward. When you invest in Canada, you can deduct substantially more of that investment immediately,” Carney said.According to the Canadian government, the measure will reduce the country’s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from about 13% to 6.4%, which it said would be the lowest among major economies and less than half the rate in the US.Carney has pledged to attract C$1 trillion in investment over the next five years by reducing red tape and developing projects in mining, energy, technology and infrastructure.He also reiterated his commitment to speeding up reviews of major projects.“Canada will remain a country of high standards. But high standards do not require slow decisions,” he said.Ottawa keeps door open to WashingtonDespite the trade tensions, Carney said around 80% of Canada-US trade remains tariff-free and suggested that a mutually beneficial agreement was still possible.“There is a mutually beneficial arrangement that can be had,” he said during a fireside chat after his speech. “When it is the right time to strike that deal, we'll be ready to do that.”Trade talks between the two countries collapsed last month before Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Ottawa retaliated, while the US subsequently announced additional restrictions on Canadian products, according to news agency AP.Carney has argued that economic integration and national sovereignty are increasingly in tension and that countries seeking to preserve their independence need to strengthen ties with like-minded partners.Europe becomes a bigger part of Canada’s strategyCarney was scheduled to travel to Europe later Tuesday, where he would address the European Parliament as Canada seeks deeper economic and strategic ties with the European Union.Canada is seeking a partnership with the EU that could include an arrangement allowing Canadians to live and work in Europe without visas, according to an AP report citing a senior Canadian official familiar with the discussions.Ottawa is not seeking EU membership or a model identical to the arrangements Norway or Switzerland have with the bloc. Instead, Canada wants a partnership tailored to its priorities, with investment at its core, the official said.About 70% of Canadian exports go to the US, making Europe central to Ottawa’s efforts to reduce its dependence on the American market.Canada and the EU already cooperate in areas including trade, defence, energy, technology and critical minerals. Bilateral trade stood at about $147 billion in 2025, making the EU Canada’s second-largest trading partner.Carney has ruled out EU membership and said Canada wants “a unique alliance” with the bloc.His European trip comes as Ottawa seeks to strengthen alternative economic partnerships while continuing to leave the door open for a future agreement with WashingtonCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Leeds data centre plan backed by West Yorkshire Mayor
articles.summary: Tracy Brabin talks to BBC Radio Leeds about data centres, tourist tax plans and a trip to India.
articles.body:
The Mayor of West Yorkshire has backed plans to build a data centre on the outskirts of Leeds.

Technology giant Microsoft has been granted permission by Leeds City Council to create the facility at the former Skelton Grange power station site in Stourton - but there is opposition to the plan.

Brabin has been answering questions as part of Message the Mayor on BBC Radio Leeds. She also talked about a proposed "tourist tax", a trade trip to India and the latest efforts to tackle domestic violence.

Read our takeaways from the interview below or listen to the full interview here .

'Big tech' will not have a blank cheque in West Yorkshire

The mayor was asked about environmental concerns around the new data centre. About 250 people gathered to protest against it in on Saturday.

"I will take each individual case as it stands - but the economic case for Skelton Grange is really powerful.

"It's about £4bn of investment in our communities; a thousand jobs.

"But 'big tech' will not have a blank cheque here in West Yorkshire. I've been very clear about that."

Microsoft says it is committed to being "carbon negative [and] water positive" by 2030.

"We will make sure that you don't pay more if you're in a lower cost hotel than in the higher-end five stars - and that families won't be impacted unnecessarily.

"But this comes on the back of the understanding that the whole of the Western world works like this.

"You go to Europe - you go to Barcelona, or Malaga, or wherever - you will pay a small amount on your room because that money then stays 'in region' and benefits the local community as well as tourists."

Mayors are being given the power to introduce an uncapped overnight visitor levy - but Brabin and other Labour mayors have agreed to set a 5% cap.

Trade trip to India is a huge opportunity

"We are selling the brand of Yorkshire. Yorkshire is five million people."

In October, Brabin will join mayors from North and South Yorkshire, and senior business leaders, on a north of England trade mission to India.

Brabin confirmed her fare will be paid for using public money and was asked whether she would fly in economy.

"Some businesses that are coming with us, they have potentially booked themselves into business [class], or some people might want to travel [in] first.

"I don't know whether I will go business or economy. Let me see."

Brabin explained she would be weighing-up whether it would be more or less cost effective to fly early in economy and spend more nights in hotels.

Elland railway station is closer to being built

"The good news is that Elland is underway and the highway and access programme has been approved, so we go to full business case.

"But yes, it's taken far too long. It's about partnership working with Network Rail and others.

"If I had a magic wand, I'd get all our stations built imminently."

Elland is finally to get a railway station, which is expected to cost £49m - more than double the original estimate of £20.3m.

A caller asked the mayor why it had taken more than 20 years to get the project started.

West Yorkshire should be the safest place to be a woman or a girl

"When I first became the mayor, violence against women and girls was our central strategy in my police and crime plan.

"We are just launching our serious violence strategy and, of course, violence against women and girls sits at the heart of it.

"Myself and our deputy mayor for policing and crime, Baroness Alison Lowe - both of us have lived experience of sexual violence.

"So we made it, obviously, a priority to get a change in our community."

articles.title: US democratic decline threatens global rule of law, report warns
articles.summary: Nearly half of US democracy indicators hit 50-year lows, accelerating global stability decline, warns new IDEA study.
articles.body:
The United States is accelerating the global weakening of the rule of law, according to a new report that found nearly half of the indicators used to measure American democracy have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years.

In the report released on Tuesday, the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA) describes the US as the “most prominent example and accelerator” of the trend, warning that its democratic erosion is having consequences far beyond the country’s borders.

“President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies ,” the report stated. “In that environment, which is marked by constricted space for both public expression and institutional checks on power, resistance is increasingly unsafe.”

Globally, around 57 percent of countries declined in at least one key indicator of democratic performance between 2020 and 2025. Judicial independence has fallen to a 36-year low, while credible elections are at their lowest level in 30 years.

But the report singles out the US because of both the scale of its decline and its outsized global influence, arguing that its retreat from democratic norms has strained multilateral institutions and emboldened authoritarian leaders elsewhere.

“The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation,” the report stated.

It pointed to Brazil and Serbia as examples, saying the aftermath of Brazil’s 2022 election, when Jair Bolsonaro sought to remain in power after losing the presidency and his supporters later stormed government buildings, “echoed” the aftermath of the 2020 US election. In Serbia, officials cited Trump’s claims of mismanagement at USAID to justify raids on civil society organisations.

“For decades, the rule of law both domestically and in the international order has underpinned the resilience of democracies,” International IDEA Secretary-General Kevin Casas-Zamora said. “Now, the rapid decline of democracy in the USA is weakening judicial independence and fragmenting the international system — threatening democracy around the world.”

The US recorded seven statistically significant declines between 2020 and 2025, including in access to justice, freedom of expression, press freedom and judicial independence. Except for free political parties, the other six are now at their lowest levels in the dataset’s history.

On press freedom, International IDEA cites cuts to funding for public broadcasters NPR, PBS and the US Agency for Global Media, as well as “ad hominem attacks on journalists, particularly women, and lawsuits against media organisations such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC”.

Universities have also come under pressure.

“Executive measures affecting funding and academic freedom in universities, including efforts to influence accreditation and hiring processes, provide a further example of the decline in Freedom of Expression,” the report said, citing the withholding of federal funds from Harvard and Columbia.

The report calls the Trump administration’s use of the immigration system the “starkest example” of declining access to justice. It points to 137 Venezuelans sent to El Salvador under the 1798 Alien Enemies Act, saying many had little or no established connection to the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang and were denied the chance to properly challenge their removal in court.

The report also warns that the broader erosion of democracy comes with consequences for global security, finding that some forms of democratic decline are associated with a greater risk of violent conflict. There were 65 violent conflicts in 2025, the most recorded since the Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s series began in 1946, including a record eight conflicts between states.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
articles.summary: The star says tour promoters took the decision, after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements on stage.
articles.body:
Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.

The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.

His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.

In his statement , Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.

"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."

He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.

The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.

In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.

Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.

However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.

Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."

In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

articles.title: Who is Jonathan Hunter Kramer? Pennsylvania man arrested with rifle, 190 rounds of fire in alleged IS-inspired plot
articles.summary: US News: Jonathan Hunter Kramer, a 21-year-old from Pennsylvania, was arrested by the FBI with weapons and ammunition, linked to a planned attack inspired by ISIS. Discover more about his past and the alarming details of his alleged plot.
articles.body: A 21-year-old Pennsylvania man is facing federal terrorism-related charges after FBI agents arrested him with a semiautomatic rifle, rifle magazines and about 190 rounds of ammunition that prosecutors say were being acquired for a planned attack.Who is Jonathan Hunter Kramer?Jonathan Hunter Kramer, from Valencia, Pennsylvania, was charged with receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing, or having reasonable cause to believe, they would be used to commit a felony or federal terrorism offence.Prosecutors allege Kramer was preparing for an ISIS-inspired attack. He appeared in federal court on September 14, with prosecutors seeking to keep him detained without bond, arguing he poses a danger to the community.2023 mass-casualty incidentKramer was previously known to the FBI following a 2023 investigation, when he was a minor. Pennsylvania authorities charged him over his role in a plot to carry out a mass-casualty incident and for possessing child sexual abuse material. He was later adjudicated delinquent.After his release from juvenile detention on March 19 this year, an anonymous tipster contacted the FBI about what they described as troubling behaviour, including Kramer ordering “mysterious” packages and reconnecting with people from before his earlier case.Investigators later linked him to an online persona called “Hamza Al Rashid”. According to the FBI affidavit, the account claimed an affiliation with ISIS, offered to share explosive manuals and discussed preparing for a “mission”. Kramer allegedly said he was only missing a “weapon”.What happened before his arrestOn September 12, FBI agents saw Kramer leave his home carrying a bag and travel by rideshare to a retail store, where he bought a disposable phone.Investigators say he then met someone in the parking lot and took a long black bag from a vehicle before travelling to a hotel in Cranberry Township, where he paid cash for a room.Witnesses reportedly heard a metallic clicking sound from the bag. Kramer later went to a sporting goods store and was seen at the gun counter by FBI agents.He was approached after returning to the hotel with two bags containing items from the store. Federal search warrants were then executed at the hotel, his home and on his person.What did investigators findAgents seized a semiautomatic rifle, five rifle magazines, a bipod and scope and about 190 rounds of rifle ammunition. Two magazines were loaded and the other three had a 30-round capacity.They also found an entrenchment tool, prayer rug, pepper spray, about 30 knives and a handwritten note that read: “Do not look for me. IDK what I did but I can’t live in constant fear”.Authorities allege the weapons and ammunition were acquired in preparation for an attack Kramer referred to as his “mission”.Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said Kramer appeared to be preparing for a mass shooting.“Kramer was taken into custody just as he appeared to be preparing for a mass shooting that could have taken many lives,” Eisenberg said.FBI Director Kash Patel said Kramer had allegedly engaged with ISIS propaganda online, developed attack concepts and expressed extremist views while acquiring weapons.What happens nextKramer faces a federal charge related to receiving a firearm and ammunition knowing, or having reasonable cause to believe, they would be used to commit a federal crime of terrorism or another felony.The complaint also refers to allegations involving the provision, attempted provision and conspiracy to provide material support or resources to a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization.Prosecutors are seeking his detention without bond pending trial.The FBI Pittsburgh Field Office investigated the case with state, local and federal agencies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Oman says
articles.summary: Iran says El Gaia caught fire after hitting mines, but the US says the oil tanker was struck by a missile and then a drone.
articles.body:
Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says.

Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula.

On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route.

But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday.

The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam.

The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February.

Also on Tuesday, Iran's semi-official Fars news agency reported that "enemy drones" had targeted two fishing boats in the strait overnight near the Iranian port of Kargan, about 80km (50 miles) north-east of Musandam.

Fars, which is linked to the Revolutionary Guards, cited the deputy governor of Hormozgan province as saying that several fishermen were reported missing following the incident and that a search-and-rescue operation was under way.

Later, a spokesman for the US military's Central Command (Centcom) told the news website Axios that its forces had destroyed two boats which tried to steal a sea drone.

"Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after Centcom forcefully responded," Capt Tim Hawkins said.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

articles.title: Can China play peacemaker as Iran’s foreign minister heads to Beijing?
articles.summary: Tehran and Beijing explore diplomatic paths amid escalating tensions between Iran and the United States.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – When Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi last visited China in May, it came shortly before a trip by United States President Donald Trump to the same country.

Araghchi is expected to be back in Beijing on Wednesday, his second visit to the Chinese capital since the US-Israel war on Iran began at the end of February. Once again, the trip comes shortly ahead of a planned meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, this time in Washington later in September

Araghchi’s own meeting on Wednesday will be with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi.

The meetings in May and now in September highlight the role China has played during the war, framing itself as a neutral party that wants an end to the conflict.

Xi urged the BRICS bloc of Global South powers during his address to a summit of member countries in New Delhi earlier this week to act as peacemakers in the Middle East conflict, and said China was willing to work with them towards that goal.

While Xi hinted at interest in potentially playing an explicit US-Iran mediation role in his BRICS speech, he did not explicitly announce any such imminent diplomatic initiative.

Instead, the Chinese president once again promoted a broad four-point plan for de-escalation in the Middle East, which is centred on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adherence to international law, and balancing development and security.

Analysts have pointed out that while China wants to see an end to a war that has brought tumult to financial and energy markets, it has traditionally avoided deeply entangling itself in third-party conflicts and potentially failed diplomatic initiatives.

Inside Iran, there have been varied opinions on the significance of Xi’s latest remarks.

Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said on Sunday that Xi’s “constructive initiatives offer timely openings to de-escalate tensions” and show that multilateral diplomacy “is the only viable path to stability”.

But Hamed Vafaei, professor of Chinese literature at the University of Tehran and a China researcher, said that perceiving Xi’s remarks as an offer to mediate between Iran and the US was more of a “free interpretation” of his words than reality.

Nuclear file, sanctions and military cooperation

Araghchi is also expected to discuss Iran’s nuclear programme with China, as Washington attempts to renew focus on Tehran’s activities.

Last week, the US and its European allies, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, successfully pushed the board of the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), to refer Iran to the UN Security Council .

The last such referral came 20 years ago and was followed by six UN Security Council resolutions being passed against Iran, and sweeping sanctions that hit the country’s economy hard.

This time, however, the move is expected to be largely symbolic. China and Russia have strongly opposed it, and can veto any new Security Council measures.

Western pressure on Tehran is continuing elsewhere. Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami was barred from attending this week’s IAEA General Conference in Vienna under “snapback” sanctions reimposed by European powers last year.

The US has continued to build on its own sanctions against Iran, launching “Operation Economic Outcast” to further isolate the Iranian government from the international community as it also tries to choke off the country through a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.

A large number of China-linked refineries, companies and financial channels allegedly facilitating dealings with Iran have also been targeted as part of the sanctions, although larger Chinese banks have not been hit so far.

But on Monday, the US Treasury designated Russia’s VTB Bank under the Iran sanctions. It did not name China in its statements, but the second-largest Russian bank is the only one with a licensed branch in mainland China, with direct access to China’s national payment system.

China remains the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil and has vowed to protect its own interests despite the sanctions. It has continued purchasing Iranian oil stored beyond the reach of the US blockade .

China’s links to Iran’s military capabilities also drew attention in the US this week, after the Wall Street Journal reported that Iran had obtained high-resolution satellite images from Chinese entities before carrying out an attack on a US military base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers.

Trump downplayed the incident when he was asked about it by reporters, saying that the Chinese were “basically doing what we do”.

“I think he’s behaved reasonably well,” Trump separately said about Xi. “When they say that China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them, too”.

articles.title: Israeli ‘influence campaign against Qatar’ launched after October 7 attack
articles.summary: Israeli newspaper Haaretz reports that influence experts and an ex-Mossad official were part of an anti-Qatar group.
articles.body:
A group of Israeli influence experts and political advisers worked on a secret campaign targeting Qatar in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, before the initiative was abruptly halted, according to a report by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.

The campaign was launched days after the assault on southern Israel and sought to pressure Qatar over its relationship with Hamas, Haaretz reported on Monday.

“Their goal was to launch a global civilian influence campaign against Qatar,” the newspaper reported.

Those behind it believed international pressure could force Doha to influence Hamas to secure the release of the 251 captives taken to Gaza on October 7.

According to the report, about 30 people were recruited to the project, including political advisers and experts in influence operations and psychological warfare.

A WhatsApp group called Free the Kidnapped was established several days after October 7. The identities of those who initiated the operation “are barred from publication”, Haaretz said.

Qatar has been the key mediator between Hamas and Israel since Israel’s genocide in Gaza began.

Although Israeli officials have repeatedly travelled to Doha for indirect negotiations with Hamas, the Israeli army carried out a missile strike on the country last year on September 9, targeting Hamas’s negotiating team. Six people were killed, including a Qatari national.

The episode was condemned by countries including France and the United Kingdom.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later apologised for the strike.

The following month, Israel and Hamas agreed to a “ceasefire” deal, which Israel to date has violated hundreds of times.

Since October, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in Gaza and injured nearly 4,700.

In total, Israel has killed more than 73,700 people since October 2023, when it launched its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.

Qatar has repeatedly denied allegations that it funds Hamas, pointing to the strict oversight governing its aid transfers.

“All our aid, financing, and all our support … went to the people in Gaza, and was a very transparent process that the United States is very aware of … [and] Israel was the one facilitating,” Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, Qatar’s prime minister, said last year . “This communication has led to ceasefires, has led to the release of hostages, has led to alleviating the suffering of the people over there.”

Doha, which has long served as a mediator in Middle East conflicts and beyond, has hosted Hamas’s political office since 2012. The decision to host the Hamas leadership came after a request from the United States, according to Qatari officials.

Haaretz reported that one member of the anti-Qatar WhatsApp group asked, “Do we know how much Qatar gives Hamas every year or some other monetary figure that we can hammer home?”

The message “Hamas is ISIS” was subsequently used on the campaign’s website and Facebook profile, the Haaretz report revealed.

Participants raised donations, produced videos, contacted journalists and arranged media appearances as part of their secret campaign.

A website was also established in several languages and social media accounts were opened.

Haaretz reported that a former Mossad official was also part of the group.

But about a month after it began, the campaign was abruptly halted.

“After a while, it was shut down. We stopped dealing with the Qatar campaign,” one participant told the Israeli newspaper. “I never heard anything more about the campaign.”

Marc Owen Jones, associate professor at Northwestern University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that there has been a campaign against Qatar for the “past three years that sounds exactly like that”.

“I’ve been tracking it,” he said. “I imagine it stopped either because they are pretending it is not happening or outsourced it to another entity for cover.

“It is unlikely such a campaign would exist without the motivation of an actor like Israel.”

articles.title: Good heavens! US reveals it has placed weapons in space
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: Space war has just come out of the closet. One small disclosure from Washington on Monday is expected to lead to a .
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Space war has just come out of the closet. One small disclosure from Washington on Monday is expected to lead to a giant leap for humankind – towards an arms race in the skies.For the first time, the United States has publicly acknowledged that it has weapons stationed in orbit, a development that confirms what space-security experts have long expected: the earth is no longer the limit; the skies will be the newest place to park weapons.“The United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed at an Air, Space & Cyber Conference near Washington, setting off concern across the world.Meink pointed to the counterspace capabilities being developed by China and Russia to assert the purpose behind the US deploying space weapons is deterrence and protection. Moscow and Beijing, and possibly New Delhi, are expected to play catch-up soon.Nobody outside classified circles knows precisely what Washington has placed in orbit. Possible counterspace weapons include jammers, systems capable of dazzling or disrupting sensors, cyber capabilities and, more controversially, kinetic weapons that can shoot and destroy satellites. The distinction matters enormously because a kinetic weapon that smashes a satellite can create thousands of pieces of debris moving at extraordinary speed, potentially threatening other satellites and spacecraft.Some experts believe non-kinetic systems such as jammers are more likely to have been deployed. Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, has suggested that the newly acknowledged American systems could be space-based jammers. The foundation's 2025 assessment says the US already had at least one offensive counterspace system deployed and was believed to have another; both were identified as jammers.But even jammers can be lethal. They can cause immense casualties on Earth without a single explosion or a missile striking a city because satellites are omnipresent now: communications satellites connect billions of people. Weather satellites help warn populations of hurricanes and other disasters. GPS supports aircraft, ships, emergency services and financial networks. Today's “We’ll be damned” may well become tomorrow’s “We’ll be jammed.”America’s journey from moonshot to slingshot in space was not unexpected. For six decades, Washington had maintained a familiar diplomatic fiction about the skies: space was becoming militarily important, but the US will not be the first to put weapons there. Russia, and more recently China, likewise essayed similar platitudes.The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but does not ban conventional weapons. The legal door was therefore never quite as firmly shut as the diplomatic rhetoric suggested. So the compact has now been gently broken, with the US announcement raising a paradox worthy of a Cold War cartoon: everybody says they want to prevent a space arms race, while donning running shoes.China reacted quickly to the development on Tuesday, urging Washington to stop “preparing for war” in outer space and warning against turning the heavens into a battlefield or triggering a new arms race. Russia likewise called for space to remain free of weapons and pressed the case for preventing its militarisation.Both countries have substantial counterspace programs of their own. China has demonstrated direct-ascent anti-satellite technology and has developed increasingly sophisticated satellites capable of rendezvous and proximity operations. Russia remains a formidable counterspace power, particularly in electronic warfare, proximity operations and anti-satellite technology, although its broader space program has suffered from economic pressures, isolation and declining launch activity.India is a more distant and quiet fourth entrant to the space club, having announced its arrival in the counterspace arena in March 2019 with Mission Shakti, when it destroyed an Indian satellite in low-Earth orbit with a hit-to-kill interceptor. Having demonstrated a credible Anti-Satellite (ASAT) capability, it is advancing rapidly in launch, docking, surveillance and space situational awareness, but its military space architecture remains substantially smaller.New Delhi said at that time the ASAT test demonstrated the country's ability to defend its space assets. Since then, India's emphasis has increasingly included space situational awareness, satellite protection and sophisticated orbital operations rather than simply blowing things up. Its 2025 SpaDeX mission demonstrated autonomous docking and undocking – a technology with peaceful applications such as satellite servicing but obvious future military utility as well. DRDO lists work involving space-based lasers, satellite jamming, electronic intelligence, rendezvous and proximity operations and space-based surveillance, moving the country toward a more sophisticated space-security architecture, while continuing to advocate negotiations to prevent an arms race in outer space.So although Russia remains highly capable in selected counterspace areas and China is the fastest-rising challenger, with India somewhere in the periphery, the US remains the most comprehensive space power. It has unmatched breadth: military satellites, intelligence, navigation, missile warning, launch capacity, enormous commercial infrastructure and an increasingly resilient constellation architecture. Its commercial space sector gives Washington another advantage: it can replenish and augment military capabilities through private companies.The immediate consequence of the American announcement though may well be psychological rather than kinetic. Some experts believe Monday’s disclosure was a deliberate attempt to seize the technological high ground after recent setbacks in terms of advances made by China and Russia in weapons development. But Beijing and Moscow are eventually expected to point to Washington's own admission when justifying further counterspace investments, heralding the arrival of another arms race – this time in the skies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
